title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, Incident Reviews, and Runbooks
author: Morgan Li
body:
Overview

Purpose
We maintain a single SRE standards reference that defines how teams (service owners, on-call, and platform) create and operate service-level objectives (SLOs), manage error budgets, plan capacity, run reliability initiatives, conduct incident reviews, and author runbooks. This document codifies our minimum expectations, ownership model, tooling, and escalation workflows.

Scope
Applies to all customer-facing and internal services in the Redwood serving plane (hosted API, Dedicated runtime, control plane), as well as critical infra dependencies (auth, telemetry, orchestration).

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

SLO principles
- Every production service must have at least one availability SLO and one latency SLO where meaningful.
- SLOs express user-facing impact (e.g., successful requests, end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency for a given route).
- Keep SLOs simple and measurable from the consumer perspective. Instrumentation must be robust (traces, request counts, latency histograms).

Required metadata for each SLO (service owner is responsible for maintaining):
- SLO name (short)
- Service and route(s) covered (e.g., model-gen-v1 /v1/generate streaming)
- Objective and window (e.g., 99.9% success over 30 days)
- Measurement method (metric name, PromQL/SQL query, primary dashboard link)
- Error budget policy (burn thresholds, mitigations, escalation points)
- Owner (primary, secondary) and paging rotation

Example SLOs
- Availability: "Generate API success"
- objective: 99.9% successful requests (2xx) measured over a 30-day rolling window. Metric: sum(http_requests{route="/v1/generate",status=~"2.."}) / sum(http_requests{route="/v1/generate"}).
- Latency: "Generate API p95 latency"
- objective: p95 < 200 ms over 7 days for non-streaming requests. Metric: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate",streaming="false"}[5m])) by (le)).

Error budget policy (standard template)
- Green: burn <= 25% \u2014 continue normal development.
- Yellow: burn > 25% and <= 50% \u2014 product manager notified; evaluate immediate mitigations (rate limiting, temporary scaling).
- Red: burn > 50% \u2014 freeze non-essential feature launches; apply remediation runbook and page SRE lead.
- Critical: burn > 80% within 24h \u2014 emergency response: critical incident process and exec notification.

Operational steps when error budget is burning
1. Owner checks SLO dashboard and alert timeline.
2. If burn enters Yellow, open a short-lived action ticket with mitigation candidates and assign owner.
3. If burn reaches Red, trigger weekly cadence: daily standups until burn stabilizes, run capacity/traffic analysis.
4. If Critical, page on-call, escalate to on-call incident process.

2) Capacity Planning

Capacity principles
- Plan for production traffic + 40% buffer for autoscaling warm-up and model inference variability unless a higher tier is contractually required.
- Use both long-term (quarterly) and short-term (weekly) planning cycles.
- Tiers: baseline (95th percentile expected load), headroom (buffer for burst), and emergency (excess capacity to handle abnormally high load).

Key inputs and signals
- Historical telemetry (90/95/99 traffic percentiles by route and model), growth forecasts (product roadmaps), upcoming marketing/sales events, new model rollouts.
- Cost per token and per-request unit economics from Finance (used to balance cost vs. overprovisioning).

Capacity planning runbook (quarterly)
1. Gather metrics: last 90 days per-route QPS, GPU utilization, GPU memory, average sequence length, p95 latency.
2. Forecast demand using linear/trend model + product inputs (documented in capacity worksheet).
3. Translate demand to GPU capacity via standard conversion table: e.g., A100-80GB supports ~X seq/s for model M under profile P. (See capacity worksheet template link).
4. Recommend reservations/scale policies: target baseline reserve commitment, autoscale thresholds, burst pool size.
5. Review with Finance and Product; publish capacity plan and target dates.

Emergency capacity steps
- If predicted GPU saturation > 85% next 72 hours, SRE triggers fast path: increase autoscaler target, enable burst pool, and if needed, migrate non-critical workloads to lower-priority queues.

3) Reliability Initiatives and Prioritization

Initiative types
- Reliability engineering (root-cause fixes, architecture changes).
- Observability improvements (missing metrics, dashboards, alert tuning).
- Operational automation (auto-remediation, canary promotion tooling).

Scoring and backlog prioritization
- Each initiative is scored by impact, effort, and risk. Mandatory high-impact items that reduce P99 latency or prevent high-severity incidents get priority. Use the Reliability Initiative Scorecard (link).
- Quarterly reliability OKRs are derived from top backlog items; teams allocate 10-20% of capacity to reliability work.

4) Incident Review Standards (Post-Incident Review / PIR)

When to run a PIR
- All Sev 1/2 incidents and any incident that consumed > 25% of an SLO error budget or had customer impact.

PIR structure (required sections)
- Summary and timeline (short blameless summary)
- Impact (SLOs affected, customer-visible symptoms, downtime/latency windows)
- Root cause analysis (technical cause and contributing factors)
- Resolution steps and timeline
- Action items (owner, due date, priority)
- Follow-up (tests, dashboards, runbook changes)

Standard PIR cadence
1. Draft PIR within 72 hours of incident mitigation.
2. Review with stakeholders within 7 days.
3. Track action items in a reliability board; verify completed items at 30 and 90 days.

5) Operational Tooling and Dashboards

Minimum dashboards per service
- SLO dashboard: real-time burn rate, historical error budget, top failing routes, and request rate.
- Capacity dashboard: GPU utilization, queue lengths, cold-start counts, autoscaler decisions.
- Observability dashboard: top traces for p95/p99 latency, recent exceptions, and downstream latency.

Alerting guidance
- Prefer SLO-based alerts (error budget burn > 25%/hour) over raw-threshold alerts.
- For infra signals: alert on GPU saturation > 90% for > 5m, queue depth > configured threshold for > 5m, and exporter CPU > 80% for > 10m.
- Tune to reduce noise: prefer multi-window detection (e.g., sustained vs. spike) and route alerts to appropriate channels.

Recommended tools and integrations
- Metrics: Prometheus + Cortex (queryable with PromQL).
- Tracing: OpenTelemetry -> Jaeger/Tempo.
- Dashboards/Alerts: Grafana with alertmanager integration.
- Incident management: PagerDuty + internal status page + Slack incident channel template.
- Capacity/runbook docs: Confluence + version-controlled runbooks in the repo.

6) SRE Runbooks (templates and examples)

Runbook format (required)
- Title
- Service and owner
- Pager/alert that triggers this runbook (link to alert)
- Impact description (what user-visible problem looks like)
- Immediate mitigation steps (1-5 numbered actions)
- Diagnostic commands and queries (copy-paste safe)
- Escalation policy (who to page next, SRE lead, product, infra)
- Post-incident actions (PIR link, follow-ups)

Example runbook: "Generate API high p95 latency"
- Pager: grafana-alert: generate-api-p95-high
- Impact: p95 latency > 400ms for > 5m for non-streaming requests; clients experience slow responses and timeouts.
- Immediate steps:
  1. Confirm alert: open SLO dashboard, check route QPS and p95 trend.
  2. Check GPU utilization across serving pool: `kubectl top pods -n serving --selector=app=model-gen` and `grafana:gpu-utilization` dashboard.
  3. If GPUs saturated > 90% and backlog growing, increase replica count or scale up instance type per capacity table.
  4. If a specific model is hot: temporarily reroute traffic to a lower-latency variant or enable model sampling with reduced beam size.
  5. If telemetry shows large queue depth, enable burst pool and communicate to product.
- Diagnostics (copy/paste):
  - PromQL: `sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route="/v1/generate",streaming="false"}[5m])) by (le)`
  - Check recent errors: `sum(rate(http_requests{route="/v1/generate",status!~"2.."}[5m]))`
  - Trace link pattern: `https://tracing.company/internal/trace?service=model-gen&time=last_30m`
- Escalation: If mitigation not effective in 15 minutes, page SRE lead and product manager.
- Post-incident: create PIR, update runbook with new diagnostics and add synthetic check for the regression.

Operational best practices
- Keep runbooks concise and runnable in the first 15 minutes of an incident.
- Test runbooks during game days at least twice a year.
- Version-control runbooks and make them discoverable from alert pages.

7) Ownership and Governance

- Service owners: define SLOs, maintain runbooks, and own PIR action items.
- SRE team: enforces standards, provides library of runbook templates, leads incident response for Sev1/2, and drives reliability initiatives.
- Product & Finance: collaborate on prioritization (cost vs. reliability) and approve capacity commitments.

8) Change log and references

- This document v1.0 published 2026-03-18 by Morgan Li; last updated 2026-04-01 to add capacity emergency thresholds.
- Reference links: capacity worksheet template, reliability initiative scorecard, SLO dashboard cookbook (internal links).

Appendix B 
\u2014 Quick checklist for new service onboarding
1. Define at least one availability and one latency SLO.
2. Create SLO dashboard and add to on-call rotation.
3. Create capacity estimate and add to quarterly planning.
4. Write initial runbook and validate in a game day.
5. Submit review for SRE sign-off.
